title: Anselm (1033–1109)
hookLine: faith seeking understanding, and God as that than which nothing greater can be thought

lines: THE FOOL HATH SAID IN HIS HEART.
cards: A monk at the abbey of Bec has already written one book about God, a long chain of arguments. Now he wants something shorter: one single argument that needs nothing else to stand on. He hunts for it, and it slips away.
He decides the hunt is a distraction and tries to stop, and the thought won't leave him alone. Then, he says, it came.
He wrote it up as a prayer, and tested it against a line monks sang in choir, in the Douay-Rheims: "The fool hath said in his heart: There is no God." The monk was Anselm.

teach.h: I BELIEVE SO THAT I MAY UNDERSTAND.
teach.b: The book is the Proslogion, and in its preface Anselm says he first titled it faith seeking understanding. The order matters.
In the opening chapter he says, in effect: I don't seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand. Faith is where he starts. Then it goes looking.
He offers a name for God: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Then he turns to the fool. When the fool hears those words, he understands them, so the idea is at least in his mind.

But if it were only in the mind, Anselm reasons, you could think of something greater: the same thing, existing in reality too. So it must exist in both. A monk named Gaunilo wrote back on the fool's behalf.
By that logic, he said, I could prove a perfect island exists just by picturing one. Anselm replied, and the objection and the reply are still read with the book.
Catholic thinkers have weighed the argument differently; Thomas Aquinas, later, did not accept it as a proof. Then the surprise.
A few chapters on, Anselm says God is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought, but something greater than can be thought at all.
A book that reaches toward God with careful logic arrives at the edge of the mind and says so.

how: Catholics honor Saint Anselm as a Doctor of the Church, and his motto, faith seeking understanding, is often used to describe the work of theology; students still read his Proslogion in philosophy and theology classes.

o: a monk who named God the greatest thinkable
a thinker who proved a perfect island exists
a bishop who wrote the first Catholic creed

p: says in his heart there is no God

s: Anselm said you must understand before you can believe
he said the reverse: he believed so that he might understand.
Anselm's argument answers a line in the Psalms
he tests it against the fool who hath said in his heart: there is no God.
Anselm thought the human mind could fully grasp God
in the same book he calls God greater than can be thought.

games.q: you've written a short book reasoning toward God. a fellow monk writes back saying your argument would prove a perfect island exists. what do you do?
o: write a reply, and let both be read with the book.
games.why: Anselm answered Gaunilo, and the objection and the reply are still read with the Proslogion.

practice: Take Anselm's phrase and turn it slowly: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Try to think of something greater, and notice where your mind runs out.
If you pray, let the thinking turn into prayer whenever it wants to; if you don't, treat it as a puzzle worth two minutes of your attention.

wordCard.voice: Anselm. A monk and teacher who called his book faith seeking understanding, and named God that than which nothing greater can be thought. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: faith seeking understanding, the title Anselm says he first gave the Proslogion.

carryVoice: Your line: faith seeking understanding. Faith starts the search; it doesn't end it. Eight hundred days now.
